The spec's last open probe was the absolute-positioning worry: whether any element anchored to a narrow assumption escapes its box once the viewport is huge. Answered by pointing the same prover T113 built for the FLOOR at the opposite extreme - control-within-viewport --width 1920 across all 23 banked pages: zero elements past the edge, zero controls off-screen. ★THE INSTRUMENT TRANSFERRED WITHOUT CHANGE because its oracle was never about small screens: it asks whether a rendering, text-or-control element extends past the viewport with no scrolling or clipping ancestor, which is a question about the BOX, not about the width - so the width became a parameter and the same gate now covers 320, 390 and 1920. Recorded as a measurement rather than an assumption so a future session does not go hunting a wide-screen break that is not there, exactly as this trajectory already did for line length. Remaining: whether dashboards DENSIFY usefully at width or merely stretch is a design judgement, deliberately not gated - the same reason width-utilisation ratchets prose measure but refuses to gate fill percentage. || Remaining: whether dashboards densify or merely stretch at width - a design judgement, deliberately not gated. || WIDE SCREENS MEASURED AT 1920 AND 2560 - NOTHING BREAKS AND LINE LENGTHS STAY READABLE (2026-08-27). 1280 is this platform's PC lane, so 1920 and 2560 are untested territory where the usual failures are content stretching into unreadable line lengths or absolute positioning coming apart. Walked 5 supervisor pages at both widths. ZERO horizontal overflow at either size. And the layout does the right thing with the extra room: the CONTAINER stretches to full width (1914 / 2554px) while the widest TEXT block caps at 610-648px, so cards and columns keep prose inside a readable measure instead of letting a sentence run the width of a monitor. ★THE ONE APPARENT OUTLIER WAS NOT ONE: project-manager showed a 1244px text block, roughly double every other page, and it is a wh-source-chip - the provenance strip ('Live - refreshed on load - updates automatically -'), a single-line metadata band that spans its card by design. My probe counted any

over 60 characters as prose, and a chip is a

. Line length matters for text a person reads line by line, not for a one-line status strip, so the readability concern does not apply to it. Remaining: whether the extra width should be USED (denser dashboards, multi-column analytics) rather than merely tolerated - a design judgement, not a measurement. || ★THE PROVER MEASURED ONE PAGE FIVE TIMES AND CALLED IT FIVE PAGES (2026-08-28). validate_width_utilisation was RED with what looked like a real regression - prose lines growing on index, analytics and pm-scheduler. Reading the raw run instead of the verdict: EVERY page reported byte-identical numbers, 99.2%% fill and 73ch 'Build a verified reputation in the' at 768, 99.7%% and 70ch 'The gap: Departments run in isolat' at 1920 - for logbook, hive, pm-scheduler alike. That prose exists ONLY in index.html. Every walk had landed on index: the prover's sign-in silently failed, every gated page bounced through whSignInWall(), and the loop measured whatever was on screen and labelled it with the page it had ASKED for. The ratchet then reported prose regressions on pages the browser never opened. ★THE BASELINE SURVIVED, which is the one piece of good design here: it is dated 2026-08-26 and contains none of index's prose, so the gate refused to ratchet a poisoned reading into the record. A failing gate that does not corrupt its own baseline is worth more than a passing one that might. ★FIX IN THE INSTRUMENT, NOT THE PAGES: the prover now compares the URL it LANDED on against the page it asked for, and ABORTS when they differ rather than attributing one page's prose to another - the same discipline prove_cold_page_teaches already applies when it refuses to measure on dirty state. Nothing about the pages was wrong; the pages were never visited. ★This is the third instrument-over-page finding of the session (with the ai-render-provenance false accusation and the cold-page abort), and they share a shape: an instrument that cannot tell 'I failed' from 'the code failed' will always report the second. || ★MEASURED AT 1920, AND THE PAGE A SUPERVISOR LANDS ON USES A THIRD OF THEIR MONITOR (2026-08-28). With the width prover's misattribution bug fixed, the first trustworthy per-page reading at this width is: index 99.7%% fill, analytics 99.7%%, pm-scheduler 99.7%%, logbook 56.7%%, and hive.html 35%%. Three pages use the whole screen; the HIVE BOARD leaves roughly two thirds of a 1920 monitor empty. That is the page a supervisor opens first and keeps open, and this trajectory's question - is the width USED or merely stretched into - has a concrete answer for it. ★AND IT IS NOT A READABILITY CAP, which would be the legitimate reason for a low fill. logbook capping at 56.7%% is defensible: its longest prose line is 52ch, comfortably inside the measure where the eye tracks well, so the narrow column is doing a job. hive is at 35%% fill while its longest prose line runs to 85ch - close to the ~90ch ceiling the gate itself names. A page that lets text run long AND leaves most of the screen empty is not protecting the reader; it is simply not laying out for the width. ★THE GATE IS RIGHT NOT TO ENFORCE THIS. Its own note says a fill percentage would be 'enforcing an opinion', and that is correct - density is a design judgement, and a dashboard that densifies badly is worse than one that leaves space. So this is recorded as a measurement for Ian rather than a defect with a prescribed fix: on a wide monitor the hive board has room for the roster, the approval queue and the feed side by side, and today it stacks them into a third of the glass. pct 70 -> 82. || LOCKING->90 2026-09-01: FINISHED (fix+gate) - all assigned gates PASS on the full board. pct -> 90. || LOCKED 2026-09-04: board gate passed. pct -> 100.

trajectories.title: Bright sunlight & the plant floor (contrast in anger)
trajectories.basis: WALKED->25 (2026-08-25, the ROUTE-state contrast method built + first run): axe color-contrast injected (vendored axe.min.js, the live-scan pattern) and run at THREE T9 route states at 390 - rest, form-dirty, asset-picker OPEN - 0 violations at every state (the critical capture path is AA-clean in the states a worker actually reads, not just page-rest). CAVEAT carried from feedback_axe_incomplete_is_a_false_100: axe's 'incomplete' set was not audited this pass - a zero needs the incomplete count read before it is a certified zero. Remaining: the incomplete-set audit, APCA-Lc floors on the route (the platform's dark-surface lens - screenshot-based per the CSSOM memory), alert/confirm elements along T19's route, dark-mode-absence posture statement (wave close).  || THE INCOMPLETE-SET AUDIT DONE 2026-08-26, and the caveat is CLOSED with one named residual. The recorded worry was right to exist: axe reports 0 violations across 26 pages AND 1,534 INCOMPLETE - 'element's background color could not be determined' - because axe cannot see behind composited alpha or a gradient, which is most of this platform. A zero over an abstention that large is a false 100 on its own. WHAT MAKES IT REAL is the second oracle, which prove_page_contrast.mjs was already driving: APCA measured 3,007 text nodes with 0 FAILING, 0 inconclusive and NO truncation, and on 23 of 24 pages its denominator is LARGER than axe's abstention set - so the nodes axe declined to judge have a verdict from an instrument built to composite alpha, average gradient stops and resolve background-clip:text glyphs. That is corroboration, not a second guess. ★THE EXCEPTION IS NAMED, NOT ROUNDED AWAY: on ASSISTANT, axe left 18 incomplete while APCA measured 15. The two counts are in DIFFERENT UNITS (axe counts elements, APCA counts text nodes), so this is NOT proof of three unjudged nodes - it is the single page where the covering argument is not clearly safe, and it is recorded as a residual rather than folded into the green. RETRIEVE-FIRST paid here: the two-oracle instrument already existed and needed no rebuilding - what it lacked was a GATE, so a contrast regression was invisible to the board. Now registered as page-contrast, which also refuses to grade a --teeth run (that mode plants deliberately failing nodes into the same report file). Remaining: APCA floors along T19's alert/confirm route, and the dark-mode-absence posture statement. || THE CONFIRM DIALOG - THE ONE STATE THE CONTRAST PROVER NEVER MEASURES - IS CLEAN, AND MEASURING IT FOUND A DIFFERENT DEFECT (2026-08-27). prove_page_contrast covers pages; it has ZERO dialog coverage (no whConfirm, modal or TARGETS reference), and while dialog provers exist for a11y, back-out, layout and session-died, none measures contrast. That matters because the confirm is where a person COMMITS - the moment bright sunlight on a plant floor is least forgiving. Measured whConfirm's own overlay at 390 with alpha composited up the ancestor chain (a naive read returns 1.00 on alpha): message 15.08:1 at 15.2px/600, Cancel 16.32:1, OK 7.88:1 - every element far above the 4.5:1 floor. Inventory's Add-Part modal measured 12.21-21:1 on the same pass. So the dialog layer is not a contrast risk, which is worth knowing rather than assuming. Remaining: the APCA route pass along T19 and the dark-mode posture statement. || ★THE PLATFORM'S ONLY CONTRAST VIOLATION WAS ON A SEEN ALERT - found, computed, fixed, re-measured (2026-08-28). prove_page_contrast across 26 pages reported exactly one axe violation platform-wide, and it was on alert-hub: '.seen > .alert-body > .alert-msg', foreground #717780 on background #131d2b, 3.75:1 at 9pt - under WCAG AA's 4.5:1, and 9pt is nowhere near the 18pt/14pt-bold allowance that would drop the bar to 3:1. ★THE ARITHMETIC EXPLAINS IT EXACTLY, which is how I knew the fix would land rather than hoping: .alert-msg is rgba(255,255,255,0.80) and .alert.seen applied opacity 0.5, giving an effective alpha of 0.40; compositing white at 0.40 over #131d2b gives R 19+236x0.40=113, G 119, B 128 - #717780, the measured colour to the byte. Raising the opacity to 0.65 lifts the effective alpha to 0.52 and the ratio to about 5.4:1. Re-ran the gate: PASS, 0 violations and 0 APCA failures over 2345 measured text nodes. ★THE DESIGN INTENT SURVIVES: `seen` exists to de-emphasise an alert somebody has already handled, and it still does at 0.65 - it just no longer dims it past reading. The person this state is FOR is the supervisor going back over what they cleared, which is precisely the moment the text has to stay legible. The opacity remains on the children rather than the card, preserving the earlier fix that keeps Unsee usable. ★NOTE ON THE TWO ORACLES: APCA reported 0 failing on this page while WCAG caught it - the perceptual model and the legal one disagreeing on the same pixels, which is exactly why this gate runs both and why 'APCA is clean' would have been the wrong place to stop looking. pct 72 -> 92. || LOCKING 2026-09-01: the fix is verified and the registered gate page-contrast PASSES standalone (re-run this session). Awaiting the next full-board earn to promote to locked. pct -> 100.

trajectories.title: Gloved hands & tremor: motor reality
trajectories.basis: WALKED->25 (2026-08-25, offset-tap tolerance probe at 390, touch context): +-12px fat-finger taps land 5/5 on the daily-path controls probed (asset-picker opener 248x46 - the 46px height absorbs the offset comfortably per the K2 floors; the PM asset card trivially). INSTRUMENT LESSON: elementFromPoint returns null outside the viewport - scrollIntoView before probing (0/5 false reads on below-fold controls first pass). The zero-width #save-entry-btn is the known form-submit shape (the offline prover's recorded lesson), not graded here. SWIPE-ALTERNATIVE CENSUS DONE 2026-08-26 (SC 2.5.7) and the platform is CLEAN - every gesture it has is one of three harmless kinds. nav-hub and companion-launcher let a person DRAG the floating button out of the way, while the button's actual job (open the hub) stays a TAP, so dragging is a convenience over a tappable control and never the only route. session-timeout listens for touchstart as an ACTIVITY SIGNAL, not a gesture requirement. wh-persona sets draggable=false, disabling dragging rather than requiring it. The one genuine keyboard trap in this family had already been closed centrally: .wh-scroll-x regions scrolled by swipe were unreachable from a keyboard (axe scrollable-region-focusable, eight of them on project-report), fixed where the shared class lives. THE GATE FOUND A HIT ON ITS FIRST RUN, and checking it rather than assuming was the right move: integrations.html registers a drop handler for CMMS imports - guarded by if (dropZone && fileInput), with a real labelled <input type=file> wired to the SAME handleFile on 'change'. Drag-and-drop laid over a working file picker is exactly what 2.5.7 asks for, so it is justified BY NAME with the reason recorded next to it. LOCKED BY gate no-drag-only, which fails on any NEW gesture-registering product file - not because dragging is forbidden, but because 'is there a tap that does the same thing?' is a question somebody must answer out loud before it ships. It is scoped to product surfaces, because a lens whose JOB is to grep for dragstart would otherwise fail a gate about dragstart - measuring the instrument instead of the product. Remaining: the JOURNEY-length tap-noise choreography (offset noise on EVERY tap of T9 end-to-end) and the precision-target sweep (checkboxes/toggles on critical paths). || PRECISION TARGETS: THE SAFETY-CRITICAL ONE IS CORRECTLY BUILT, AND THE REST ARE BEHIND DIALOGS (2026-08-27). 24 checkbox/radio inputs exist platform-wide; 5 carry class="hidden" and are styled through their labels, which is the right pattern rather than a defect. ★THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST CHECKS OUT: logbook's LOTO / Permit-to-Work checkbox - the control that records whether energy was locked and tagged out before someone put their hands in a machine - renders a 20px box (w-5 h-5), and it is wrapped in <label for="f-loto" style="min-height:44px"> spanning the icon and the text, so the TAP TARGET is 44px even though the visual is 20. Small visual, large target: exactly the discipline a gloved hand needs. logbook's Status radiogroup is the same shape - visually-hidden radios with sibling <label for=> pills doing the tapping. ★MY FIRST TWO MEASUREMENTS WERE BOTH WRONG, IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS. The live probe reported ZERO precision targets across six pages, which was offsetParent skipping controls inside collapsed forms - not absence. Then a static pass reported 10 visible checkboxes 'without a 44px label', including three with NO label at all - which was my regex searching BACKWARD for a WRAPPING label and never considering a sibling <label for=>, the very pattern the status toggle uses. The correct rule is the UNION of the input's box and any label bound to it, wrapper or for=. ★WITH THAT RULE, ONLY 1 CONTROL IS MEASURABLE AT REST (on resume, and it passes): the rest genuinely live inside dialogs and sheets. So this is measured for the always-visible set and OPEN for the dialog set - and the move is the existing dialog_targets harness rather than a new opener. Remaining: run the precision sweep THROUGH dialog_targets, plus the journey-length tap-noise choreography. || SWEPT THROUGH THE DIALOG HARNESS TOO - REUSED, NOT REBUILT (2026-08-27). Drove tools/dialog_targets.mjs (50 registered targets, each carrying its real opener path) at 390, measuring newly-revealed checkbox/radio controls before and after each open so only genuinely dialog-gated ones count. Result: 1 further precision target revealed and it clears 44px, so across everything currently measurable - always-visible plus dialog-revealed - ZERO controls sit under the gloved floor. ★THE REMAINDER ARE GENERATED PER ROW, and they use the same correct pattern: logbook's .pm-task-check and #tasklist-ack-check both ship class="hidden" and are tapped through their labels, so measuring the INPUT would report a 0x0 box for a control whose real target is a full-width row. This platform's precision discipline is consistently 'small visual, large target', and the LOTO checkbox is the clearest instance of it. ★WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM: the per-row generated controls in populated task lists are still unmeasured, because reaching them needs data plus interaction rather than an opener - so this is 'zero failures wherever measurable', not 'zero failures'. The distinction is the whole point of this session's instrument lessons. Remaining: the per-row sweep over a populated PM task list, and the journey-length tap-noise choreography. || ★THE TAP-TARGET FLOOR IS CENTRALISED AND CORRECT ON THE AXIS MOST IMPLEMENTATIONS MISS (2026-08-28). A gloved hand on a plant floor is the persona this trajectory exists for, and the 44px floor is the single most consequential thing for it. It is centralised - tokens.css and components.css both carry it - and applied across 41 files, replacing what the source itself records as 'inline min-height:44px hand-added on 12 pages'. ★THE DETAIL THAT MAKES IT REAL: the canonical class sets BOTH AXES, and the comment says why - 'F1 fails on the MIN dim'. WCAG 2.5.8 measures the SMALLER dimension, so a button 200px wide and 30px tall fails while a min-height-only rule would call it compliant. That distinction is the difference between passing a checklist and actually being tappable with a work glove, and somebody knew it. It also uses inline-flex so short labels still centre inside the enlarged box, which is what stops a floor rule from making the UI look broken - the reason such rules usually get removed again. ★WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED HERE is the harder half: this trajectory wants a fat-finger INJECTION - tap offsets applied along a real journey - and swipe-dependent interactions checked for tap alternatives. A CSS floor proves the targets are big enough; it does not prove a gloved worker completes T9's logging flow without mis-hits. That needs the offset-noise choreography this trajectory specs. pct 72 -> 84. || LOCKING 2026-09-01: registered gate no-drag-only re-verified PASS standalone (static, read-only). Awaiting board earn for locked. pct -> 92. pct -> 100.

trajectories.title: Low battery & power-save mode
trajectories.basis: WALKED->25 (2026-08-25, measured idle-network audit): index makes ZERO network requests during a full idle minute post-boot (armed request listener, 60s window) - no polling loops, battery-clean at rest on the landing/ops-home; the known 15s-poll lives on hive.html (its focus-preservation lesson already banked) and realtime uses websockets, not polls. prefers-reduced-motion is honored via the Q1 dims. Remaining: the CPU-throttle lane (Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate 4x-6x) on the T9 core journey - the earlier NETWORK throttle prover proved loopback throttling non-binding, so CPU is the honest power-save proxy; animation-fallback completeness under reduced-motion; the idle audit swept across the other wall-candidate pages (wave close).  || THE IDLE AUDIT SWEPT ACROSS THE ROSTER 2026-08-26, and the first run of it was WRONG in the most instructive way. Eight pages, watched with zero interaction: SEVEN are completely silent, and alert-hub makes ~11 requests per 75s from setInterval(loadAll, 60000) - roughly 500 an hour if left on a wall. ★THE FIRST RUN WATCHED FOR 45 SECONDS AND REPORTED ZERO ON ALL EIGHT, including alert-hub, because a 60-SECOND POLL NEVER FIRES INSIDE A 45-SECOND WINDOW: the cleanest-looking result in the sweep was the page that polls hardest. A window shorter than the thing it measures produces a zero that means nothing, and banking it would have recorded the wall-display candidate as the quietest page on the platform. The window is now 75s, longer than every interval in the served roster. ★AND THE PAUSE IS PROVEN RATHER THAN TRUSTED: what makes a 60s foreground poll defensible instead of a battery leak is that it STOPS when nobody is looking - alert-hub does wire visibilitychange to stopRefresh - so the probe hides the tab and asserts silence. Measured: 0 requests in 75s hidden. A poll still running in a backgrounded tab is invisible to every foreground measurement, which is exactly why it needed its own assertion. Scope stated honestly: WEBSOCKETS are not visible to this probe, so a zero means 'no polling', never 'no activity'. LOCKED BY gate idle-network, forward-only per page. Remaining: the CPU-throttle lane on the T9 core journey, and animation-fallback completeness under reduced-motion. || ANIMATION-FALLBACK COMPLETENESS UNDER REDUCED-MOTION — MEASURED 2026-08-27, and the answer is that nothing is lost. The worry was real and specific: an animation that is DISABLED rather than skipped-to-its-end leaves content in its pre-animation state, which for anything styled opacity:0 is the identical 'page loads, content invisible' failure T119 found on index and community, reached through a different door. Swept 12 pages with prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, counting every RENDERED element that carries its own text and computes to opacity 0. Result: the only such element anywhere is #wh-hub-current-label. ★AND THE CONTROL IS WHAT MADE THAT A RESULT RATHER THAN TEN FINDINGS: re-run with reducedMotion 'no-preference', the SAME label is opacity 0 on the same pages. It is the nav hub's collapsed-label design - the label fades in when the hub expands - not a motion-preference failure. Without the control this would have been filed as ten pages hiding text from reduced-motion users, which is exactly the shape of false finding this arc has been correcting all day. ★A GENUINE OBSERVATION FELL OUT OF IT: index renders MORE text under reduced-motion (1061 chars) than without it (525), because the stagger branch fires everything immediately instead of waiting for scroll. The reduced-motion path is the more COMPLETE one, which is the right direction for it to err. Remaining: the CPU-throttle lane on the T9 core journey. || THE CPU-THROTTLE LANE — WALKED 2026-08-27, the last item this trajectory named. T37 throttles the NETWORK; power-save mode and a cheap phone throttle the PROCESSOR, which is a different failure surface: JS-heavy pages degrade by dropping work, not by waiting. Drove the T9 core logging journey at a 4x CPU slowdown via CDP Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate. RESULT: the entry form was present at 1856ms, the page rendered, voice-handler loaded, and - the assertion that matters - the VALIDATION STILL FIRED: submitting with no asset produced 'Please select an asset before saving.' rather than silently dropping. A refusal that goes missing under load is worse than a slow one, because the worker believes the entry saved. Zero page errors throughout. So the 8%-battery scenario this trajectory was written for is a working scenario, not merely a slower one. Combined with the idle-network gate (nothing polls in a backgrounded tab) and the reduced-motion sweep (no content hidden, verified against a control), the power-save story is measured on all three axes it has: what the page DOES while idle, what it SHOWS when motion is off, and whether it still WORKS when the processor is slow. || Remaining: nothing owed beyond the wave-close re-earn - idle-network, reduced-motion and the 4x CPU lane are all measured. || INDEPENDENTLY RE-CHECKED, AND THE TWO ALARMS WERE BOTH MY SCAN (2026-08-27). Swept every setInterval on the platform: 11 across 10 pages, of which only alert-hub pauses on visibilitychange - which reads like ten pages polling in a pocket at 8% battery. Two looked alarming and neither is. logbook's 250ms interval SELF-CLEARS - `if (tryRegister() || ++tries > 20) clearInterval(t)` - so it is a bounded five-second retry waiting for a registration, not a poller. analytics' '400' was never an interval period at all: my regex read the setTimeout NESTED INSIDE the callback, while the actual interval is 2800ms and is held in _loadingInterval so it can be cleared when loading ends. The remaining long intervals (60s on alert-hub, platform-actions, skillmatrix; 10s on marketplace) are the cadence this platform already chose and documented. ★SO 'ONLY ONE PAGE PAUSES WHEN HIDDEN' IS TRUE AND MOSTLY HARMLESS, because most of the others are not running anything while hidden - a bounded retry has already finished, and a loading rotator stops when its content arrives. Counting setInterval CALLS measures how many exist, not how many RUN, and those are different questions. This confirms the existing idle-network finding rather than reopening it. || ★SEVEN PAGES SIT AT ZERO WHILE IDLE; THE EIGHTH READING IS CONTAMINATED BY MY OWN PROBES (2026-08-28). Measured with prove_idle_network, a 75-second watch per page. index, logbook, pm-scheduler, inventory and dayplanner each issued ZERO requests while nobody touched them, and alert-hub issued exactly 11 - matching its recorded baseline to the request. For a platform whose worker is at 8%% battery at the end of a shift, an idle page that costs nothing is the right answer, and seven of eight deliver it. The static picture agrees: only 11 pages use setInterval at all and the busiest cadence is 10s. ★THE EIGHTH: hive.html reported 14 requests against a baseline of 0, and I am NOT banking that as a regression, because the run was not clean. hive.html carries FOUR postgres_changes subscriptions - it re-reads when the database changes - and during this watch I was myself writing to the database: the import-undo prover creating and rolling back rows, and my own deletions of the leftover T175 probe account and the WH-EFFECT-PROBE audit row. Its busiest endpoint was /rest/v1/logbook, a feed re-fetch, which is exactly what a realtime handler does when someone else writes. Every OTHER page matched baseline exactly, including alert-hub's distinctive 11 - so the instrument was working; the subject was being disturbed. ★A page that reacts to real changes is not idle-costly, it is CORRECT; the measurement only means anything in a quiet database. The prover has no page-scoping flag, so re-taking it means another full run in a window with no other probes - which is the honest next step rather than either banking a regression or waving it away. This is the same discipline as the T158 stale-feed number and the T86 outbox backlog: a true reading of a subject I had disturbed. pct 90 -> 90. || ★THE HIDDEN-TAB FAILURE NEEDS THE SAME CAUTION - the pause it accuses alert-hub of lacking is ALREADY THERE (2026-08-28). The gate's verdict reads 'alert-hub kept POLLING while the tab was HIDDEN - 15 requests in 75s', and its reasoning is right in principle: a 60s refresh is correct for a board somebody is watching and a battery leak in a pocket. But alert-hub already implements exactly that pause, deliberately and with the reason written in: a visibilitychange listener that calls stopRefresh() when document.hidden, and loadAll()+startRefresh() when it comes back, sitting under the comment 'Pause polling while the tab is hidden (mobile + battery friendly)'. The prover simulates hidden correctly too - it overrides visibilityState AND hidden and DISPATCHES visibilitychange - so the handler does fire. ★THE ARITHMETIC SAYS THE TIMER IS NOT THE SOURCE. loadAll() issues 7 database calls, and alert-hub's only setInterval is the 60-second one - in a 75-second window that is at most one or two cycles. 15 requests is about two loadAll()s, in a window where the timer was stopped. What alert-hub also has is FOUR realtime channels, whose handlers re-read when the database changes and do not consult visibility - and I was writing to the database throughout this run (probe deletions, the import-undo prover). Event-driven re-reads triggered by my own writes explain the count; a stopped timer does not. ★SO TWO THINGS ARE TRUE AND NEITHER IS 'THE PAUSE IS MISSING': the measurement was contaminated exactly as hive.html's was, AND there is a real open design question underneath it - whether a realtime handler should ALSO stand down while the tab is hidden. That is not obviously yes: pausing realtime is how an alert board stops being an alert board. It needs a clean re-run first, in a quiet window, and then a decision rather than a patch. I twice today came close to editing correct code on a bad reading; this is the third and the same discipline applies. || ★RESOLVED, AND MY CONTAMINATION THEORY WAS WRONG: THE PROVER WAS COUNTING BOOT TRAFFIC AS IDLE TRAFFIC (2026-08-28). Two runs of prove_idle_network on unchanged code disagreed wildly - index reported 0 requests, then 12; logbook 0, then 3; pm-scheduler 0, then 9. I first guessed my own concurrent database writes were firing realtime handlers. That is refuted by the decisive fact: index.html has ZERO setInterval and ZERO realtime channels. It cannot poll and it cannot react - by construction it has no mechanism to generate a single request while idle. So its 12 requests were not idle traffic at all. ★THE MECHANISM IS THE SETTLE WINDOW. The prover waits a FIXED 8 seconds after domcontentloaded before it starts counting, on the reasoning that 'boot traffic is not idle traffic' - correct reasoning, wrong implementation. On a loaded host (this session has run browser provers continuously) a page's data reads arrive later than 8s, land inside the 75-second watch, and are counted as idle cost. The busiest endpoints give it away: v_logbook_truth and logbook and pm_assets are BOOT reads, not refresh endpoints. A constant settle measures the MACHINE as much as the page, and the baseline's zeros were simply captured on a quieter one. ★FIX: wait for networkidle (30s cap) instead of a fixed delay, with the 8s wait kept as a fallback for pages that never fully settle because a live subscription holds the socket, plus a 1.5s beat after quiet so a trailing read lands inside boot rather than inside the watch. ★AND THIS RETIRES THE TWO 'FINDINGS' ABOVE: hive.html's 14 and the alert-hub-hidden 15 were the same artifact, which is why alert-hub appeared to poll while hidden despite having a correct, deliberate visibilitychange pause. Neither was a battery leak. The honest position on this trajectory's core claim - that idle pages cost nothing - is that it needs re-measuring with the corrected prover before it can be asserted OR denied. || ★MEASURED CLEANLY WITH THE CORRECTED PROVER - the platform's idle profile is excellent, and the code was right all along (2026-08-28). With networkidle replacing the fixed 8-second settle, the readings are finally about the PAGES: index 1 request in 75s (a single google-analytics beacon, which is legitimate and not a data read), and logbook, pm-scheduler, inventory, hive, dayplanner and analytics all at ZERO. Seven of eight surfaces cost a backgrounded phone nothing at all. alert-hub sits at 11 while VISIBLE - its declared 60-second refresh, one loadAll of seven reads, exactly as designed and stable across every run today. ★AND THE HIDDEN-TAB TEST NOW READS: 'alert-hub HIDDEN for 75s: 0 requests (poll paused - correct)'. The visibilitychange handler works precisely as its comment promised. Earlier this session the same test reported 15 requests and accused this page of leaking battery in a pocket; I came close to editing a correct, deliberate pause on the strength of it. What saved that code was checking the MECHANISM before the verdict - index.html has zero timers and zero subscriptions, so its '12 idle requests' were impossible, and an impossible reading indicts the instrument rather than the page. ★So this trajectory's central claim - that a worker at 8%% battery pays nothing for a page nobody is touching - is now VERIFIED rather than asserted, and the verification is repeatable because the settle no longer measures how busy the computer is. pct 90 -> 96. || ★STATUS fixing -> locking (2026-08-31), and the pct does NOT move. trajectories.title: The old browser floor
trajectories.basis: WALKED+FIXED->60 (2026-08-25): THE FLOOR DEFINED by feature census - ES2020 (optional chaining pervasive: 470 uses in engineering-design.js alone; Promise.allSettled in project-manager; no ES2022 features found) = pre-Chrome-80/WebView-80 (~2019 budget Androids) engines FAIL AT PARSE, and no canary/noscript existed anywhere - the failure mode was a wordless white page. FIXED (first slice) + VERIFIED: browser-floor.js - a pure-ES5 canary (eval-probes `?.`/`??` so the parse error throws instead of killing the script) that paints an EN+FIL role=alert banner naming the remedy ('update Chrome / Android System WebView from the Play Store'); wired into index.html BEFORE any modern script (the entry door); proven: parses as ES5, loads on index, banner correctly ABSENT on a modern engine. SWEEP DONE same-day: 39 more pages wired (verified on logbook/pm-scheduler/hive: canary loads, no false banner, zero pageerrors; offline-fallback + status deliberately excluded as ES5-lean). Remaining: the support policy stated on status/help, the sw-registration path on old engines, a floor-browser Playwright lane for the positive test (banner PRESENT on an old build) (wave close). DEPLOY NOTE: new file browser-floor.js ships with the release. POLICY STATED 2026-08-26: the supported-browser FLOOR is now readable by a user or IT admin - status.html carries a 'Which browsers WorkHive supports' block (2020-or-newer engine: Chrome/Edge 80+, Safari 14+, Firefox 74+, updated Android System WebView) naming what the canary does on an older engine and the remedy. Status is the right home: it is where someone goes when something will not work, and it LOADS under total backend outage (verified in T71's probe). 'Degrade defined, not discovered' needed the definition READABLE, not only enforced in browser-floor.js. Remaining: sw-registration path on old engines, a floor-browser Playwright lane for the positive test. || THE OLD-ENGINE PATH — TESTED BY REMOVING THE CAPABILITY, 2026-08-27, and it found a real defect on the most important page. I cannot install a 2023 Android WebView, so I did the local-substitute thing this roadmap already uses elsewhere: strip the APIs an older engine lacks (serviceWorker, IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver) before any page script runs, and walk. SERVICE WORKER: clean on all five pages - nav-hub.js guards with `if (!('serviceWorker' in navigator)) return;` and simply does not register. INTERSECTION OBSERVER: index.html THREW 'ReferenceError: IntersectionObserver is not defined', and the consequence was not a missing animation. `.reveal` starts at opacity:0 and is only shown when the observer adds `.visible`, so the throw meant 14 elements stayed INVISIBLE FOREVER - the landing page rendered 525 characters of text where every other page rendered 1146+. ★NOTHING WOULD HAVE REPORTED THIS, because the page 'loaded fine': no failed request, no error state, no blank shell - just content that never faded in. Same shape as a skeleton that never resolves. And the code SAID it was safe: the comment above the observer read 'all browsers', which is an assumption wearing the clothes of a check. FIXED at all five call sites, each failing OPEN rather than silently: the main reveal adds `.visible` to everything, the stagger reuses its EXISTING reducedMotion branch (which already fires everything, so no second code path was invented), the before/after rows are shown outright, and the sticky-CTA and nav-highlight observers - which only ADD behaviour - return early. The nav-highlight one was the loudest, constructing an observer PER SECTION. VERIFIED BOTH WAYS: without the API index now renders 1061 chars and no page throws; with it, the observer still fires and .reveal elements still gain .visible on scroll, no errors. Remaining: a floor-browser Playwright lane for the positive test. || GATE animation-never-hides-content REGISTERED. ★AND THE REGISTRY GATE CAUGHT ME FIRST: I set this trajectory to 'locking' with the fix landed but NO gate built, and validate_trajectory_registry.py refused it - 'locking MEANS the gate is built, so either register it or drop back to fixing'. That is the registry declining to let a status overstate the work, which is exactly what it is for; the honest move was to build the gate rather than to soften the status. It requires BOTH halves of the property, because a guard alone is not enough - skipping the observer while leaving opacity:0 in place would pass a naive 'is it guarded' check and still ship a blank page - so every construction needs a feature check BEFORE it (positional: a check that runs after the throw protects nothing) AND the hidden class needs a reveal-everything fallback. Teeth 4/4, including one negative whose EXPECTATION was wrong on the first run: I asserted that removing the first guard should read clean because later guards remain, and the gate correctly reported a finding. The gate was right and my test was wrong. || THE SWEEP WIDENED TO ALL 23 PAGES, and found a SECOND page of the same class plus one finding that was mine. COMMUNITY: its virtual list expands .vcard-stub placeholders into real posts via renderIO, so without the API _initObservers() threw and NO stub was ever expanded - the feed was a column of empty placeholders, 1043 characters against 2691. Fixed to fail open, and the fix took TWO tries: a bare early return swapped the ReferenceError for 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading observe)', because eight OTHER call sites do renderIO.observe as posts arrive, are filtered, or are prepended by realtime. The working shape is STAND-IN observers whose observe() expands the stub immediately - which is what 'observe' means with no virtualisation - so even stubs added after load become real cards. Now renders 4868 characters, MORE than with the API, because every post renders rather than only the near-viewport ones: slower on a long feed, and a slow feed beats an empty one. Virtualisation verified intact on a modern engine (16 stubs / 4 cards at load, 6 / 14 after scrolling, no errors). ★AND ONE FAILURE WAS THE PROBE'S: report-sender appeared to throw 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading register)', but it guards correctly with `if ('serviceWorker' in navigator)` - my simulation had defined the property with a getter returning undefined, so the `in` check passed while the value was missing, a state NO real browser is ever in. The probe now DELETES the property, and report-sender is clean. I nearly filed a defect against a page whose guard was already right. All 23 pages now degrade cleanly. Gate roster widened to both pages, 6/6 teeth including one proving it BITES on community rather than passing it vacuously. || Remaining: a floor-browser Playwright lane for the POSITIVE test; the negative direction (APIs absent) is proven across all 23 pages. pct -> 94. pct -> 100.

community.html: the virtual list fails open - stand-in observers whose observe() expands a stub immediately, so a feed with no IntersectionObserver renders every post instead of empty placeholders

trajectories.title: Cross-device continuity: phone ↔ PC same account
trajectories.basis: the account-vs-device SPLIT documented (substrate/reference/state_scope_registry.json): account = identity + persona (worker_profiles) + memberships + all records; device = G5 filters, X2 drafts, offline queues, ACTIVE HIVE selection, language/TTS, one-shot notices - each with its rationale (deliberate, not accidental). Known tensions named: notification read-state device-local (T107), phone-drafts invisible on PC with no in-app statement. Remaining: parity checks per row + the drafts-live-where-typed statement surfaced in-app (wave close). THE STATEMENT SURFACED 2026-08-26 - the registry's own open tension closed. Drafts are DEVICE-local by design (they must survive an offline session, which account-level sync cannot promise), but nothing said so, and a worker who starts a note on the phone and opens the PC finds an empty box and reasonably concludes the work was lost. whAutoSaveDraft (the CENTRAL helper, every adopter at once) now announces it ONCE per browser and ONLY when a draft actually comes back: 'Drafts live on the device you typed them on, so this one will not appear on your other devices.' - an explanation at the moment it explains something, never a nag. PROVEN live on dayplanner: typed, reloaded, focused, draft restored and the flag set. state_scope_registry.json updated to record the closure. Remaining: parity checks per row, notification read-state cross-device (T107's lane). || LANGUAGE IS PERSON-SCOPED BY NATURE AND DEVICE-SCOPED BY STORAGE, SO IT FAILS BOTH WAYS (2026-08-27). worker_profiles carries exactly one preference column - preferred_persona - so the platform already decided that a companion choice belongs to the PERSON and follows them between devices. Language did not get that treatment: it lives only in wh_lang in localStorage, and sign-out's clearIdentityHard does not touch it (correctly - it clears the eight identity keys and nothing else). ★THAT BREAKS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AT ONCE. Same person, second device: a worker who set Filipino on the station tablet opens their own phone and gets English, with no indication their choice existed. Different person, same device: on the shared tablet this platform is built for, the next worker inherits the previous one's language. For a product whose stated audience is Filipino plant workers, the setting most tied to whether someone can READ the screen is the one that does not follow them - while the choice of AI companion voice does. ★THE FIX PATTERN IS ALREADY IN THE SCHEMA: preferred_persona shows how a person-level preference is stored and synced, so this is adding a sibling column rather than inventing a mechanism. Recorded on both T120 (the account-vs-device scope split) and T45 (the Filipino lane), since it is one fact with two owners. Not applied: a schema addition is a migration, and migrations land deliberately - flagged rather than slipped in mid-session. ★CORRECTION (2026-08-27, same session): the language finding above OVERSTATED itself. substrate/reference/state_scope_registry.json already catalogues 'language EN/FIL, TTS toggles' as DEVICE-level with the rationale 'device context (a shared tablet may serve FIL speakers)'. So it is a considered decision, not an oversight: on the station tablet this platform is built for, the language belongs to the STATION and its crew, and syncing it per-person would flip the screen's language on every sign-in - the opposite of helpful for a Filipino-speaking crew sharing one device. What survives is much smaller: a worker who sets FIL on the tablet and then opens their OWN phone sets it once more there, which the registry's own logic accepts. ★AND THIS IS THE THIRD TIME TODAY THE CODEBASE HAD ALREADY REASONED ABOUT WHAT I FLAGGED - analytics' comment explaining why it refuses role=tab, the psql probe pinning why no rest-day model exists, and now this registry entry. The pattern is clear enough to be a rule: before recording a design gap, look for where this platform wrote down its decision, because it usually did. || THE STATE-SCOPE REGISTRY WAS RECORDING ONE AXIS OF THREE - NOW UPDATED (2026-08-27). The registry is this trajectory's whole instrument: 4 account-level rows, 7 device-level, 3 tensions all closed, each with a rationale. It is thorough about WHERE state lives and silent about WHOSE it is: no mention of __owner (T121's shared-tablet stamp), none of __hive (added this session), and no row for logbook's page-local wh_logbook_draft store, which never goes through the shared helper at all. So a reader could consult the SSOT for remembered state and come away believing a draft is scoped by DEVICE, when it is scoped by device AND person AND plant. ★UPDATED: drafts and filters now name their within-device scope and the reason each stamp exists (a hive-A filter matches nothing in hive B and renders an EMPTY LIST, which this platform has trained people to read as 'there is nothing here'); the drafts row now names BOTH stores rather than implying one; a new row records exam progress as owner-scoped and deliberately NOT hive-scoped, since a welding exam describes the person and hive-scoping it would lose a contractor's attempt at every site switch. _meta now states the general rule: device-vs-account is the FIRST axis, and a row naming only its store answers where the state lives without answering who may see it back. Remaining: the per-row parity checks and notification read-state cross-device (T107's lane). || ★ONE PREFERENCE TRAVELS; EVERYTHING ELSE IS PER-DEVICE; NOTHING SAYS WHICH (2026-08-28). Enumerated the split this trajectory asks about. ACCOUNT-level: preferred_persona, a worker_profiles column read on load by assistant, index and voice-journal, so a companion choice follows the person to any device. DEVICE-level: wh_lang (written from three pages), wh_asset_view, wh_analytics_filters, drafts - and wh_community_last_seen, the bound the unread badge is computed against. ★THE READ-STATE ONE IS THE MOST FELT. There are NO server-side read-state columns anywhere in the schema (no last_seen_at, last_read_at, seen_at or read_at), so 'what is new to me' is a fact about a BROWSER, not about a person. A worker who reads the community on their phone walks to the shared station tablet and is told the same posts are new; clearing it on one device clears nothing on the other. On a plant floor where one tablet is shared and everyone also carries a phone (T121's reality), that is the difference between a badge people trust and one they learn to ignore. ★AND THE SPLIT IS UNSTATED, which is this trajectory's actual complaint: nothing labels which preferences travel, so a user cannot predict it and the next preference added has no rule to follow. Language has the strongest claim to being account-level after read-state - it is a fact about the reader, not the hardware - while filters and view memory are defensibly per-screen. ★Recorded rather than built: moving read-state to the server is a schema addition plus a write on every visit, and moving wh_lang is a one-line change with a real product question attached (should changing language on one device change it everywhere?). Both are Ian's, and the measurement above is what makes them decidable. pct 72 -> 86. || LOCKING 2026-09-01: BUILT + registered lock gate state-scope-registry (account/device split well-formed; active-hive device-level, identity account-level); teeth + real-file PASS. pct -> 90. ||2026-09-02 PROMOTED locking->locked by post_board_promote on the full board (1043 PASS / 24 FAIL, mode full; all named gates PASS). pct -> 100.

trajectories.title: The shared device (one phone, many workers)
trajectories.basis: serial-user probe ran (A types a private draft -> signs out -> B signs in, same device): NO UI leakage - the per-worker draft key (wh_logbook_draft_<name>) keeps B's form clean; identity keys clear on sign-out. THE TENSION: A's draft TEXT survives sign-out in localStorage (readable via devtools on a shared device). Purging on sign-out would destroy legitimate work (X2's whole point - shift-end sign-outs), keeping it is a shared-hardware exposure - a SCOPED DECISION for Ian (e.g. a purge-my-drafts option on sign-out). Recorded in state_scope_registry known_tensions. Remaining: filter/journal leakage sweep + switch-friction timing (wave close). THE LEAKAGE SWEEP FOUND A REAL, PLAIN-SIGHT LEAK - AND IT IS FIXED (2026-08-26). Walked the actual shared-device sequence (the plant reality: one tablet at the station): worker A typed a private note, signed OUT, worker B signed IN, opened the same page and FOCUSED the field - A's words were sitting in B's compose box, submittable under B's name (attribution poison on top of the privacy break). Measured leftovers after sign-out: 5 personal keys including the draft payload, wh_worker_name, wh_last_worker and hive name. ROOT FIX, not purge: whAutoSaveDraft now STAMPS each draft with its owner and REFUSES to restore one belonging to somebody else - A's work is preserved (it returns for A) while B never sees it, which purge-on-sign-out could not have achieved. Legacy unowned drafts are deliberately not restored: a one-time cost in the safe direction. PROVEN live A->B->A: B sees '', A returns to their own note, 0 pageerrors. This closes the registry's own known_tension #3 by a better route than the scoped purge decision it proposed. Remaining: identity-key leakage beyond drafts (filters/journal), switch-friction timing. FILTER HALF CLOSED same pass: whAutoRememberFilters now carries the same owner stamp. Two reasons, both real on a station tablet - a filter LEAKS INTENT (a supervisor filtered to one person's name) and, more plainly, worker B inherited A's filter and met a list that looked empty or wrong with no explanation. PROVEN A->B->A on logbook: A sets 'Mechanical', B inherits '', A returns to 'Mechanical'; the g5d-reauth-restore gate still PASSES, so same-user restore across re-auth is untouched. || IDENTITY-KEY LEAKAGE BEYOND DRAFTS — FOUND AND FIXED 2026-08-27, and it was the AI CONVERSATION. companion-launcher.js persisted chat turns under wh_ai_history_global - the default key is literally the string 'global' - and repainted them into the widget on load. The file contained ZERO references to wh_last_worker, wh_worker_name or __owner, so the store had no notion of who typed it. On the plant reality this platform is built for (ONE tablet at the station, workers signing in and out through a shift): worker A asks the companion about a machine, a mistake, or a person; A signs out; B signs in, opens any page, and A's conversation is sitting in the widget. ★THE PLATFORM ALREADY KNEW THIS LESSON AND HAD APPLIED IT ONE STORE OVER: whAutoSaveDraft stamps every draft with its owner and refuses to restore someone else's, written for this exact scenario in the compose box. The lesson simply never reached the chat history - which is the same shape as today's other sibling misses (the silent XP path, the second discipline/category refusal, analytics-report's page-break rule). FIXED with the identical model, deliberately rather than inventively: stamp on save, refuse on load, PRESERVE A's history for A. Purge-on-sign-out would have destroyed real work; ownership does not. ★AND IT TOOK BOTH READ PATHS: a second read went straight to localStorage, bypassing the loader, so stamping the store alone would have left the one path that actually paints the widget on boot still restoring another worker's words. PROVEN LIVE on one device: planted as Leandro Marquez (owner stamped, 1 turn), same worker still sees it, then as Bryan Garcia the loader refuses (wouldRestoreOthersHistory false) while A's history REMAINS on the device for A's return. Legacy unowned entries are not restored - a one-time cost, and the safe direction. Launcher verified clean on five pages. Remaining: switch-friction timing. || AND THE REST OF THE PER-PERSON KEYS SWEPT, so 'leakage beyond drafts' is now ANSWERED rather than half-checked. storage_key_registry.json's 35 canonical keys yield six per-person candidates; each was opened rather than guessed at. wh_analytics_filters is ALREADY owner-stamped - JSON.stringify({ ..._filters, __owner: _anOwner() }) - so someone had carried the lesson there. wh_asset_view holds a view MODE ('worker' | 'engineer'), wh_pm_recent_<HIVE_ID> a hive-scoped recently-viewed list, and wh_voice_journal_persona a persona choice that is cloud-synced per account anyway. ★THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS IS CONTENT vs PREFERENCE: a preference surviving a shift change is harmless and on a shared station device arguably desirable - the next worker gets a sane default, and nothing private is revealed. A recently-viewed list scoped to the HIVE names only things both workers can already open. What must never survive is somebody's WORDS. So the AI conversation was the single real gap in the set, it is closed, and the remaining unowned keys are unowned CORRECTLY rather than by omission - which is the difference between a swept surface and an unexamined one. Remaining: switch-friction timing (how long a sign-out/sign-in actually costs at shift change). || SWITCH-FRICTION TIMING — MEASURED 2026-08-27: 672ms from handover (identity cleared) to a usable sign-in field. Under a second, on the interaction a shared plant tablet performs at every shift change and often several times a shift. That number matters because friction here is what drives the ACTUAL failure this trajectory exists to prevent: if switching were slow, workers would simply not switch, and every entry would be filed under whoever signed in first - the mis-attribution session-timeout.js was written to stop. A sub-second handover makes doing the right thing cheaper than not doing it. The field is username-based rather than email, which suits field workers who often have no email at all. Remaining: nothing owed beyond the wave-close re-earn - ownership of drafts, filters and AI history is settled, the preference-vs-content line is drawn, and the handover cost is measured. || A SECOND SHARED-DEVICE CARRIER, FOUND BY ENUMERATING EVERY STORAGE KEY RATHER THAN THE ONES I ALREADY KNEW (2026-08-27). 22 distinct localStorage keys are written platform-wide. Sign-out's clearIdentityHard removes exactly EIGHT - wh_last_worker, wh_worker_name, workerName, wh_active_hive_id, wh_hive_id, wh_hive_name, wh_hive_role, wh_hive_code - which is the right list for IDENTITY, and drafts are deliberately preserved by ownership rather than purged (this trajectory's own fix). The other fourteen survive a user switch. For genuine PREFERENCES that is defensible and probably correct on a station tablet: wh_lang staying Filipino, wh_asset_view keeping the engineer toggle, wh_voice_journal_persona - these belong to the DEVICE and its crew. ★BUT THE DISMISSAL FLAGS ARE NOT PREFERENCES: wh_onboarding_dismissed, wh_cmms_guide_dismissed and wh_onb_audit_visited record that A PERSON has already been shown something. On the shared tablet this platform is built for, the SECOND worker to use it - often the newest hire, the one who most needs it - never sees onboarding, because somebody else dismissed it before they ever signed in. The guidance is not withheld by a decision about them; it is withheld by a decision about a colleague. ★AND wh_analytics_filters CARRIES TOO, which is the empty-list confusion again: B opens analytics filtered to A's selection and reads the result as the data. Both are the same shape as the draft leak this trajectory already fixed - state that belongs to a PERSON living in a store keyed only to the DEVICE. Remaining: decide per key whether it is device-scoped (keep) or person-scoped (stamp or clear) - the dismissal flags read as person-scoped and the analytics filters as person-scoped; that is a small, statable policy rather than a per-page sweep. || ★THE LAST PERSON-SCOPED KEYS WERE THE DISMISSAL FLAGS, AND THEY LEAK THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION FROM EVERY SIBLING (2026-08-28). This trajectory's recorded remainder was 'decide per key whether it is device-scoped or person-scoped'. Walking the shortlist found the content keys already swept - wh_ai_history_ stamps and refuses, wh_analytics_filters stamps AND checks on read, drafts and filters carry __owner/__hive - and three flags left storing the literal '1', which belongs to the BROWSER: wh_onboarding_dismissed (index's first-run ladder), wh_cmms_guide_dismissed (integrations), wh_guide_link_dismissed_<page> (learn-link's chip, on EVERY page). ★WHY THESE SURVIVED THE SWEEP THAT FIXED THEIR SIBLINGS: the draft, filter and history fixes all stopped A's CONTENT reaching B, so they read as privacy work and this did not - nothing of A's is exposed. What crosses is A's DECISION, and it lands on B as an ABSENCE: no card, no chip, nothing on screen to notice or report. The onboarding ladder is the sharpest case - its three step-checks were ALREADY person-aware (workerName, jobs, pmDoneToday), so it knew B had done nothing; the flag simply returned before the check ran. Correct logic behind a device-wide gate. Fixed CENTRALLY: whStateOwner() replaces a FOURTH hand-rolled owner read (_fOwner/_draftOwner/_anOwner/_historyOwner had each rewritten the same three lines), plus whIsDismissed/whSetDismissed, and all three sites route through them. A legacy '1' is nobody's, so the guide returns ONCE - for HELP that is the safe direction, since re-showing costs a tap and hiding costs the introduction. sessionStorage flags exempt (they die with the tab). Live-proven at 390: A dismissed -> B sees the guide -> A still dismissed (preserved, not purged) -> legacy '1' belongs to no one; probe captured the real owner first and restored it. GATE a-dismissal-belongs-to-a-person registered, selftest 9/9 - including two NON-VACUITY checks, because the first version of both negatives swapped only the helper CALL and left the typeof guard inside the exemption window, passing while detecting nothing. Remaining: nothing owed beyond the wave-close re-earn. || ★THE SHARED-DEVICE LEAK THAT MATTERS IS ALREADY FIXED, AND FIXED THE RIGHT WAY (2026-08-28). This trajectory's sharpest probe is leakage between serial users of one station tablet - drafts, filters, journal. DRAFTS: solved, and the reasoning is recorded at the site in the exact terms this trajectory uses ('one tablet at the station, workers signing in and out'). The scenario was real: A typed a private note, signed OUT, B signed IN, focused the field, and A's words were in B's compose box where B could submit them UNDER THEIR OWN NAME. The chosen fix is OWNERSHIP rather than purge-on-sign-out - stamp the draft with whoever typed it and refuse to restore someone else's - explicitly because purging 'destroys real work'. A's draft survives for A; B never sees it; legacy ownerless drafts are not restored at all, called out as 'a one-time cost, and the safe direction'. T57 later added an AGE stamp too, after a draft typed three months ago restored exactly like one typed three minutes ago. ★HIVE CONTEXT IS ALSO CLEARED between identities - resolveActiveHiveContext wipes all six hive keys up front 'so identity B never inherits identity A's hive', a cross-tenant leak already closed. ★WHAT IS NOT OWNER-SCOPED: whRememberView keys plainly, so remembered FILTERS, tabs and view selections do carry from A to B. Recording that as the low-severity item it is rather than inflating it - a remembered 'show only critical' is preference state, not content, exposes nobody's words, and on a station tablet is arguably convenient. The journal is DB-side under RLS, so it is not a localStorage question at all. pct -> 78. || ★PCT FIELD CORRECTED DOWN TO MATCH THIS BASIS (2026-08-31). The field read 99 while the basis's own last word was 78 - a later note revised the number and only the prose was updated. Every one of the six rows found this way was inflated, never deflated, which is the direction drift always takes when nothing checks it: the number a reader trusts drifts up while the narrative underneath it says otherwise. Now gated by pct-matches-basis. || ★LOCKED 2026-08-31: the wave-close re-earn landed and every gate this row names read PASS on a FULL board (draft-survives-reauth,a-dismissal-belongs-to-a-person). That was the only item its basis still owed. pct 78 -> 100. pct -> 100.

trajectories.note: ★THE DRAFT SURVIVES ON A THREE-LINK CHAIN NOBODY CAN SEE IN ONE PLACE (2026-08-27). whAutoSaveDraft saves the text; clearIdentityHard wipes only IDENTITY keys; and the restore is gated by an OWNER CHECK reading wh_last_worker - the key the expiry just deleted. It works solely because sign-in writes that key back. Re-key the check to anything sign-in does not restore and every draft is silently discarded after an expiry, with an empty form and no explanation. Gated by draft-survives-reauth, which asserts the chain resolves (at least one live link, since the check is a fallback chain whose alias is a documented dead read) and that expiry wipes no draft key. The owner check itself is the shared-tablet protection and must stay: removing it would 'fix' expiry by leaking one worker's typing to the next person on the device.

trajectories.title: Interruption storm: the phone rings mid-everything
trajectories.basis: WALKED->25 (2026-08-25, injected interruption at the half-typed-form step, worker 390): BOTH halves GREEN - (1) visibilitychange-hidden + pagehide(persisted) for 3s then return: every field intact; (2) the harder half, a FULL RELOAD (the OS-killed-tab case): BOTH fields restored from the whAutoSaveDraft autosave ('62Hz' probe text back in place, restore note visible). The X2 machinery holds at this step. STEP-PARAMETERIZED SWEEP BUILT 2026-08-26, and it CORRECTED THIS ENTRY'S OWN ATTRIBUTION. The line above credits 'the whAutoSaveDraft autosave' for the logbook restore - LOGBOOK DOES NOT USE THAT HELPER. It has its own saveDraft/restoreDraft on DRAFT_KEY. That mattered more than tidiness: the shared helper received OWNER STAMPING in T121, so one worker's draft cannot surface for the next person on a shared plant phone, and logbook - the platform's richest personal-text form - was never touched by that fix. CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: logbook is safe anyway by a different route, because DRAFT_KEY is 'wh_logbook_draft_' + WORKER_NAME, so the next person's page computes a key it simply cannot read. Two mechanisms, one guarantee - now written down, before someone 'unifies' them and removes a protection they did not know was there. THE SWEEP: the wizard is filled progressively and a FULL RELOAD (the OS killing a backgrounded tab, the harshest realistic case) is injected at the END OF EACH of the three steps. Result 3/3, every field back. Mutation-proven with restoreDraft disabled - 0/3, every lost field named - so the green means something. AND THE PROBE'S FIRST RUN PRODUCED A FALSE FINDING I did not bank: it reported 'the draft lost f-root-cause', which is a <select> where assigning a value that is not one of its options silently yields empty. Nothing had been set, so nothing could be lost. The probe now ABORTS on a value that did not take rather than grading a field it never filled. LOCKED BY gate interruption-steps. Remaining: mid-photo-upload interruption, 30-minute-away variants, and the lock-screen privacy-flash probe. || THE 30-MINUTES-AWAY VARIANT, MAPPED - AND ONE HALF OF MY OWN MEASUREMENT WAS TOO CRUDE TO BANK (2026-08-28). Only a page showing live PLANT state needs to age visibly. ★AND THE COLUMN THAT WOULD HAVE IDENTIFIED THOSE - 'does the page state its freshness' - WAS UNRELIABLE, so nothing is banked from it. My regex looked for 'as of / last updated / refreshed on load / Live -' and scored shift-brain FALSE, which would have made the most operational page on the list look like the worst offender. Recorded: the refresh-path map is sound and reusable; the freshness-statement audit is NOT done. Remaining: that live freshness walk over the operational subset, plus the mid-photo-upload interruption and the lock-screen privacy-flash probe (both hardware-ish). || THE LIVE FRESHNESS WALK RAN AND THE ANSWER IS CLEAN, WITH TWO NUANCES WORTH KEEPING (2026-08-28). Walked the eight OPERATIONAL pages signed in and read what a person can actually see, matching any phrasing that dates the data rather than the four I had guessed. SIX state it at rest, through a consistent idiom - 'Live - refreshed on load - Based on your PM assets, PM tasks & PM completions' plus a 'How this is computed' expander on pm-scheduler, dayplanner and inventory; analytics carries 'Updated 1h ago' AND 'Generated: <date> - Period: last 90 days'; index dates every row ('Electrical - 51d ago'); alert-hub says 'No brief was generated for this shift'. TWO read SILENT and NEITHER is a defect: shift-brain is silent because no plan exists for this shift, and a plan that was never generated has no generation time to show - the correct empty state, not a missing stamp; asset-hub HAS the idiom (5 references in source) but behind its two-gate reach, the same view-toggle-then-select that its detail view needs, so a resting walk cannot see it. ★BOTH NUANCES WOULD HAVE BEEN FILED AS DEFECTS BY THE COUNT ALONE - one is an honest empty state and the other is my probe not reaching the surface, which is the same pair of mistakes this session has made repeatedly in other clothes. The freshness-statement question from the previous entry is now ANSWERED and the earlier grep-based column stays retracted: adoption is complete across the operational subset. Remaining: mid-photo-upload interruption and the lock-screen privacy-flash probe, both needing real hardware. || ★DRAFT PROTECTION IS UNIVERSAL, MEASURED - 13 of 13 typed-entry surfaces (2026-08-28). The premise of this trajectory is that an interruption must never cost typed work, so the first question is coverage, and it is complete: every page carrying BOTH a client write path and a textarea - assistant, community, dayplanner, founder-console, inventory, logbook, marketplace, marketplace-seller, platform-actions, pm-scheduler, project-manager, resume - uses whAutoSaveDraft, between one and five instances each. Zero gaps. ★AND THE ONE PAGE MY INSTRUMENT EXCLUDED WAS THE ONE THAT MATTERED MOST. voice-journal has a textarea and NO client .insert, so the coverage scan skipped it - not a flaw in the page but a fact about it: its row is written SERVER-side inside voice-journal-agent, which is precisely the coupling T12 recorded, where a 429 on the AI reply means the note is never stored. Checked separately, it is protected too, and protected CORRECTLY: whAutoSaveDraft('voicejournal-type') plus the discipline stated in its own comment - 'Clear the draft only on a CONFIRMED save. On a failure the text stays in the draft, which is the whole point of keeping one.' That is the right semantics for the one surface whose write can fail for reasons the worker cannot see, and it means a quota-drained Friday costs a reply, not a note. An exclusion is worth reading: the page a coverage scan drops is often the page whose shape is unusual, which is where the interesting risk lives. ★WHAT REMAINS NEEDS INJECTION, NOT READING: the probes about TIMING breadth (background 30 seconds versus 30 minutes and return) and mid-UPLOAD interruption on the photo path cannot be settled from source - a draft that exists is not proof a draft SURVIVES a 30-minute eviction, and the photo case has no draft at all by nature. Those want the visibility/pagehide choreography this trajectory specs, parameterised per flow step. trajectories.title: The copy-paste & autofill reality
trajectories.basis: flagship (join code) hardened BY CONSTRUCTION: input handler uppercases + strips non-alphanumerics on every input event (padded/lowercase/newline paste normalizes), autocapitalize=characters, maxlength=6, Enter submits, M2 inline validation with aria-invalid. Auth autocomplete attrs pre-verified (T1 arc). PASTE GAUNTLET RUN ON THE NUMERIC FIELDS 2026-08-26 - and the headline finding was MINE AND WRONG, caught by my own resurrection before it was banked. The first measurement set el.value = '1,500' directly and watched the field empty with validity VALID; I wrote that up as 'pasting a thousands separator silently empties the box'. Running the finished prover against the PRE-FIX utils.js then passed FOUR OF FIVE cases: with a real clipboard, Chromium's paste pipeline already strips the comma, the spaces and the trailing unit before sanitization. ASSIGNING a value and PASTING one are different mechanisms, and only one of them is what a person does. The registry says so plainly rather than keeping the louder claim. THE DEFECT THAT SURVIVED IS REAL BUT NARROW: an UNPARSEABLE paste ('abc') blanks the field and says NOTHING - and in a quantity box a silent blank is easy to miss while the consequence is submitting no quantity at all. whCleanNumericPaste (utils.js, one delegated document-level listener so it reaches inputs any page renders later) now announces instead. Its normalization of separators/whitespace/units is recorded as HARDENING, not a measured fix: it makes the behaviour the platform's own rather than one engine's undocumented filtering, and whether other engines empty the field is UNMEASURED - only Chromium is installed. Also caught while writing it: the helper originally used a LOOKBEHIND regex, which is ES2018 - a browser lacking it throws a SyntaxError while PARSING utils.js and takes every page down. Rewritten with a capture group. And the heredoc that wrote it silently turned a \b into a literal backspace character, which would have made the thousands rule never match - the same escape-corruption class this project has a standing rule about, caught by reading the bytes back. LOCKED BY gate numeric-paste (5 cases, real clipboard - a synthetic ClipboardEvent produced a THIRD false reading, because the already-clean case falls through to the native paste and a synthetic event has no clipboard behind it). Remaining: the non-numeric half of the gauntlet (part numbers, emails) and the password-manager profile run. || THE NON-NUMERIC HALF WALKED AND IT IS VERIFIED-GOOD, WITH THE PROPERTY NOW LOCKED (2026-08-28). Scanned every page for free-text reaching a payload UNTRIMMED and then read each hit rather than banking the count: 4 hits, 2 of them FALSE - inventory's q and cat are the remembered-filter SNAPSHOT, restored into the input and re-trimmed at the point of use (line 1042), so judging by the assignment instead of the use would have filed two defects against correct code. The 2 real ones are dayplanner's note and logbook's knowledge, both free-form textareas where leading whitespace is CONTENT rather than an accident - correctly left alone. Every field where whitespace changes an ANSWER already trims: si-username, su-username (twice, with toLowerCase), the inventory search, part_number, part_name, and report-sender's contact-email. ★NOTE THE PLATFORM SIGNS IN BY USERNAME, NOT EMAIL - I went looking for si-email and there is none, which is the sort of assumption that quietly produces a gate pointed at nothing. GATE a-pasted-identifier-still-matches registered, selftest 7/7 with each field mutated independently, and its selftest mutates COPIES after a first version that rewrote real product files and restored them in a finally block - one crash from a corrupted source. Remaining: the password-manager profile run (needs a real manager, hardware-ish). pct -> 100.

fixes: utils.js: whCleanNumericPaste + delegated paste normalizer, announces an unparseable paste

trajectories.title: Print reality (the clipboard-and-paper plant)
trajectories.basis: WALKED+FIXED->60 (2026-08-25): the print census found print CSS on ONLY project-report (2 blocks) - pm-scheduler (the page plants PIN TO A BOARD), analytics, audit-log, logbook all printed as dark dashboards (navy toner floods, nav/FAB chrome, sheets in flow). FIXED + VERIFIED on the highest-value target: pm-scheduler now carries @media print (white body, black text, chrome/buttons/overlays display:none, cards bordered + page-break-inside avoid) - proven via print emulation (body rgb(255,255,255), FAB hidden, zero visible buttons) + an A4 PDF snapshot (.tmp/t124_pm_print.pdf). Remaining: the printable-set decision (analytics? audit-log? logbook day-sheet?) + the same block applied there, PDF-exporter vs browser-print parity, page-break sanity on long schedules (wave close). PRINTABLE SET DECIDED + APPLIED 2026-08-26. The set, chosen by what a plant actually carries on paper: pm-scheduler (the shift's PM list), project-report (already had print CSS), logbook (the day-sheet taken to the morning meeting) and audit-log (dispute evidence - the one surface someone prints to hand to another person). Analytics is deliberately OUT: a screen-read whose charts print as ink blocks, and whose numbers reach paper through the report sender. Print CSS added to logbook + audit-log (chrome hidden, white ground, table page-break rules) and VERIFIED live under emulateMedia('print') on all three: bodyBg rgb(255,255,255), color rgb(17,17,17), ZERO visible buttons. INSTRUMENT LESSON (two false readings before the true one): the first probe read the SW-cached copy, the second read index.html because logbook bounces a SIGNED-OUT visitor to the sign-in wall - a print check must block the SW *and* sign in, or it measures a different page and reads its own setup as a page defect. Remaining: PDF-exporter vs browser-print parity, page-break sanity on a long schedule. (2026-08-26, same pass: the printed pages now carry T125's context stamp - hive, person, printed-at - so the paper identifies itself.) || PAGE-BREAK SANITY ON A LONG SCHEDULE — MEASURED 2026-08-27, and it was a real defect on two pages. project-report's daily-progress table carried `table.doc-table { page-break-inside: avoid }`. Grown to 96 rows under emulateMedia('print') it stood 5049px tall — roughly FIVE A4 pages — while the rule asked the browser to keep the whole thing on one sheet. That is an instruction no engine can honour, and the way they fail it is to push the entire table onto a fresh page and overflow anyway: a wasted sheet and a risk of clipping the end. `avoid` belongs on things SHORT BY CONSTRUCTION — a signoff block, a clause, a result tile — never on a table that grows with its data. FIXED on both project-report and analytics-report (`.doc-panel table` had the identical rule, found only because the gate was widened past the held set — the same fix-every-path shape as the second discipline/category refusal and the silent XP sibling earlier today). The row-level `tr { page-break-inside: avoid }` is what actually protects paper and stays. ★AND THE HEADER NEEDED NO FIX, WHICH I CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: <thead> computes display:table-header-group and nothing overrides it, so it already repeats on every printed page — 'add a thead rule' would have been a change with no effect dressed as a fix. ★THE RESURRECTION PROOF EARNED ITS KEEP: the first RED run came back GREEN, because the selector capture had swallowed the /* explanatory comment */ above the rule, and that comment mentions <thead>, so the row/cell exemption fired and skipped the real declaration — a matcher grading my prose instead of the CSS beneath it. Comments are stripped before matching now, and the proof is honest: RED (exit 1) naming `table.doc-table, .signoff-block` against the pre-fix world, GREEN (exit 0) on HEAD. Remaining: PDF-exporter vs browser-print parity. || PDF-EXPORTER vs BROWSER-PRINT PARITY — RESOLVED 2026-08-27. resume.html is the only surface carrying BOTH paths (html2pdf and window.print). They LOOK divergent: downloadPDF() captures the LIVE #resume-paper node, printResume() writes a FRESH document. But both derive from the SAME buildResumeHTML(), and renderPaper() sets the node's innerHTML wholesale from it, so the only way they could disagree is an in-place edit inside the paper — and measured live, the paper contains ZERO editable nodes (no contenteditable, input, textarea or data-basics). Parity therefore holds by CONSTRUCTION, not by luck; the remaining differences are deliberate page geometry (html2pdf margins [10,10,12,10]mm and a pinned 680px content width vs @page margin 14mm). ★AND THE WALK FOUND SOMETHING BIGGER THAN PARITY: on a fresh account the preview offered FOUR exports — PDF, Word, Print, JSON, all enabled — over a resume whose entire content was the 15-character name. Checked the database before calling it empty rather than after (resume_versions: 0 rows), because a preview showing only a name could equally have been data failing to render, which is the worse bug. A one-line PDF is worse than a refusal: it is a file the person can send. FIXED with a notice in the overlay CHROME — deliberately NOT inside #resume-paper, since that node is exactly what html2pdf captures and a warning printed onto the artifact would BECOME the artifact. ★THE FIRST CUT OF THAT CHECK SILENTLY FAILED ON THE ONE CASE IT EXISTS FOR: it measured paper.innerText, and renderPaper() runs while the overlay is still display:none — for an element that is NOT BEING RENDERED, innerText falls back to textContent, which swept in the inlined <style> block and measured 1820 characters of CSS as if it were resume content. The note stayed hidden on precisely the empty resume it was written for. Now it walks the real children and skips <style>, stable whether or not the node is on screen. Both branches proven: empty -> warns (0 chars of body), populated -> silent (80 chars), with the CSS excluded in both. || Remaining: nothing owed beyond the wave-close re-earn - PDF-vs-print parity is resolved (shared builder, zero editable nodes) and the page-break defect is fixed on both report pages. || ★LOCKED 2026-08-31: the wave-close re-earn landed and every gate this row names read PASS on a FULL board (print-is-readable-on-paper). That was the only item its basis still owed. pct 95 -> 100.

fixes: project-report.html + analytics-report.html: page-break-inside:avoid moved OFF the growing data tables and kept on the rows (and on the signoff block / clauses / tiles that are short by construction)
resume.html: the preview warns when the resume is still empty, in the overlay chrome (never inside #resume-paper, which is what html2pdf captures)
